newsitem.title: INDIA: India truckers continue strike after talks fail.
newsitem.headline: India truckers continue strike after talks fail.

text.p: Indian truck owners on Wednesday said talks with the government had broken down and continued with a 10-day-old nationwide strike that has paralysed trade and pushed up prices.

"Talks have broken down. No agreement has been signed, so the agitation continues," S.P. Singh, spokesman of the All India Motor Transport Congress (AIMTC), told Reuters. Earlier on Wednesday, Singh had said a deal was expected to be reached.
Singh said the talks broke down after AIMTC officials met government officials in the Finance Ministry. He did not give reasons.
Earlier, he said the government had agreed to the truck-owners shedding their responsibility to collect a five percent service tax and also agreed to keep a hike in insurance premiums in abeyance.

The truckers, representing 2.2 million vehicles, had launched the strike against the tax and the premiums, which they said were too high. The tax was proposed by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in his budget for the fiscal 1997/98 (April-March).
There was no immediate response from the government though government officials had said earlier on Wednesday that they expected to narrow the areas of disagreement soon.
"Positive negotiations are going on," Yogendra Narain, the highest-ranking civil servant in the Surface Transport Ministry, told Reuters earlier on Thursday.
AIMTC's secretary-general, Chittranjan Dass, said in a statement on Tuesday the government and the truck owners had reached a draft agreement which fell short of the demand to remove the service tax.

The centre-left coalition of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, fighting for its life after the Congress party withdrew its support, has said it cannot rescind the tax because the budget proposals are before parliament and yet to be approved.
The budget is being held hostage by the political crisis. Deve Gowda faces a confidence vote on Friday.
"If the budget is not passed, then the whole problem would be solved," Singh said. "But still we have to wait and watch."
Narain said the transport of essential commodities had been satisfactory in most states.
"Prices have certainly not risen substantially," he said. "But the strike has definitely affected industry and ports."
S.V. Damankar, secretary of the Bombay Port Trust, which is among India's busiest ports, said cargo handling had fallen off to 3,000 tonnes a day compared with the usual 250,000 tonnes.
Analysts said businesses that depend on agricultural produce were the worst-hit as movements had been restricted.
"The economy is losing at least 70 billion to 80 billion rupees ($1.9 billion to $2.2 billion) per day," K.R. Vishwanathan, a senior economist at the Birla Economic Research Foundation, told Reuters.
